name: Göbekli Tepe
hook: Megaliths in Turkey show hunter-gatherers built monumental enclosures before farming began.
claim: Klaus Schmidt found monumental Pre-Pottery Neolithic stone enclosures at Göbekli Tepe, built by pre-agricultural hunter-gatherers from the late 10th millennium BCE. His further reading of the site as purely ritual 'temples' with no residents is tracked as a separate candidate.

claimed_age.label: ~9600-8200 cal BC
claimed_age.basis: AMS radiocarbon on collagen, charcoal and lime mortar, mostly run at Kiel. E.g. mortar KIA-44149: 9984+/-42 BP = 9745-9314 cal BC; latest PPN activity 8860+/-60 BP = 8240-7780 cal BC.

accepted_age.label: ~9600-8000 cal BC
accepted_age.basis: DAI synthesis (Clare 2020): Layer III circular/oval enclosures (PPNA, from ~9500 cal BC) underlie Layer II rectangular buildings (PPNB, to ~8000 cal BC); no re-dating has overturned the original PPNA start.

orthodoxy_at_claim.label: Standard models held that a farming economic base was needed to support large-scale monumental construction; hunter-gatherers were not expected to build it.

unambiguous_signal.note: Multi-ton carved T-shaped pillars in walled circles are unambiguous artificial construction. The 'purely ritual, no residents' reading was an interpretation of that evidence, later revised (S7).

documented_context.note: Excavated in place from 1995 by a trained DAI/Şanlıurfa Museum team under Schmidt, with stratigraphic layers (III under II under I) documented from the outset.

multiple_dating_methods.note: Lithic typology suggested a PPN date before excavation, but typology is itself cross-dated by radiocarbon elsewhere, not independent here. Radiocarbon was the only method applied at the site.

multiple_labs.note: Reported radiocarbon codes (e.g. KIA-44149, KIA-44701) all carry the Kiel AMS laboratory prefix; no independent replication by a second dating laboratory was found in the sources reviewed.

professional_recovery.note: Excavated under permit by Klaus Schmidt (German Archaeological Institute) jointly with the Şanlıurfa Museum from 1995.

peer_reviewed_report.note: Schmidt's preliminary report on the 1995-1999 excavations appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Paleorient in 2000.

material_accessible.note: No independent (non-DAI) study of the material within about five years of the 1995 claim was found; the first outside critique (Banning) did not appear until 2011.

independent_teams.note: One coordinated DAI-Şanlıurfa Museum project; no second team added evidence within five years. Comparable T-pillars at Nevalı Çori (Hauptmann) are corroborating context, not independent evidence.

proponent_stake.note: Academic, institutionally funded excavation (DAI/Şanlıurfa Museum); no commercial, religious or nationalist motive documented. The popular 'world's first temple' framing outran the evidence (S7).

objections.text: Before Göbekli Tepe, monumental or ceremonial construction was thought to require a farming economic base to support the necessary labor and surplus.
objections.outcome_note: Neither domesticated plants nor animals are documented at Göbekli Tepe's Layer III (S3); hunter-gatherers organized monumental construction before agriculture. Now standard in the literature.

objections.text: Large-scale coordinated monumental building was also thought to require a sedentary, resident population, not seasonally mobile foragers.
objections.outcome_note: Domestic-type structures with hearths were later found beside the enclosures (S7), implying some on-site residency, but these are not yet radiocarbon-dated against the enclosures' main use.

objections.text: The evidence for calling the enclosures exclusively 'temples', with no domestic buildings anywhere on site, is equivocal.
objections.outcome_note: Post-2014 excavation (S7) found domestic-type round-oval structures with a hearth sequence beside the enclosures; DAI calls revising the 'temple' framing 'unavoidable'. Whether the enclosures are houses is untested.

objections.text: The large enclosures' fill was first read as deliberate, ritually-motivated backfilling when each fell out of use; if so, dates and finds recovered from fill would not represent primary construction or use.
objections.raised_by: Excavation team, revising Schmidt's original reading
objections.outcome_note: S7: fill is redeposition from slope slides off adjacent knolls, containing mixed PPNA/PPNB material; explains heterogeneous fill dates. Finds like S9's skull fragments cannot be dated to a single phase.

status_note: Core claim vindicated: the ~9600-8200 cal BC age and building by pre-farming hunter-gatherers are widely accepted; no re-dating challenges them. Schmidt's 'temple, no residents' reading did not hold (S7) and is split out.
refinements: Function reinterpreted: 2015-19 excavation found domestic-type buildings with hearths and rainwater harvesting beside the enclosures; the DAI calls revising the 'temple' framing unavoidable (Clare 2020).
Chronology refined to an 8-phase sequence: Layer III circular-oval enclosures (PPNA, from ~9500 cal BC) lie under Layer II rectangular buildings (PPNB, to ~8000 cal BC) (Clare 2020).
Enclosure fill, first read as deliberate ritual backfilling, is redeposited slope-slide debris mixing PPNA and PPNB material (Clare 2020), which explains the scatter of fill dates.
Over 7,000 grinding and pounding tools and phytolith evidence show large-scale cereal processing on site (Dietrich L. et al. 2019), supporting mixed use of the site.
Modified human skull fragments point to a Neolithic 'skull cult' (Gresky et al. 2017); a burial (DR1) found later revised the 2017 view that burials were absent (Clare 2020).
what_settled_it: Radiocarbon dates from 1998 and Schmidt's 2000 peer-reviewed report placed the enclosures in the PPNA, and no re-dating has challenged this. Layer III has yielded no domesticated plants or animals (Dietrich et al. 2012), so the builders were hunter-gatherers.

timeline.event: 1963 Istanbul-Chicago survey (Benedict, in Cambel & Braidwood) records flint-strewn knolls with small cemeteries at the site; significance not recognized.
Schmidt, recognizing the slabs as prehistoric megaliths, begins excavation under the DAI and Şanlıurfa Museum; the first T-shaped pillars are uncovered.
First radiocarbon dates from the site are obtained.
Schmidt publishes a preliminary report on the 1995-1999 excavations, describing monumental T-pillar enclosures and an unusual 'religious' character.
Edward Banning publishes 'So Fair a House,' arguing the enclosures may be domestic buildings rich in symbolic content rather than exclusively temples.
Dietrich, Heun, Notroff, Schmidt and Zarnkow synthesize evidence, proposing feasting and possible beer brewing (oxalate spot tests; stated as not yet certain).
Klaus Schmidt dies; DAI research at the site is subsequently coordinated by Lee Clare, who directs renewed excavation and reassessment.
Gresky, Haelm and Clare report modified human skull fragments, evidence for a Neolithic 'skull cult'; no formal burials found at the site.
Dietrich L. et al. report over 7,000 grinding/pounding tools and phytolith evidence for large-scale cereal processing at the site.
Clare's DAI review and Kinzel & Clare's synthesis describe a revised, 8-phase chronology and call for revising the popular 'world's first temple' framing.

decisive_tests.test: Complete micromorphological/use-wear study of excavated Layer II rectangular buildings to determine what fraction show domestic markers (hearths, storage, bedding) versus only symbolic/ritual features.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether domestic occupation was site-wide and continuous or limited to specific structures or phases, resolving how much of the complex functioned as ordinary housing.

decisive_tests.test: AMS-date organic material (phytoliths, faunal collagen) from primary floor deposits inside the large decorated enclosures themselves, rather than fill or mortar, at a second laboratory outside Kiel.
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the enclosures' primary-use dates reproduce independently of the project's usual dating laboratory, and match the accepted ~9600 cal BC start.

decisive_tests.test: AMS-date short-lived material (e.g. hearth charcoal) from the domestic-context hearth sequence reported in S7 and compare against the enclosures' wall-mortar dates (e.g. KIA-44149, S6).
decisive_tests.would_show: Whether the domestic structures are contemporary with the enclosures' main use (mixed ritual-domestic site) or postdate them (supporting a purely-ritual Layer III).

falsifier: Independent re-dating placing the enclosures after regional adoption of domesticated cereals or livestock, or domesticates found in primary Layer III contexts, would overturn 'monumental building before farming'.

sources.note: Abstract read via OpenAlex: evidence for exclusively cultic/temple buildings is equivocal, possibly resting on ethnocentric sacred/profane distinctions; buildings may be houses rich in symbolism.

sources.note: Full text (DAI PDF): domestic structures, hearths, rainwater harvesting (2015-19); fill is slope-slide redeposition (mixed PPNA/PPNB), not ritual backfill; burial DR1 mapped; undated by AMS.

sources.note: DOI and citation confirmed via Crossref; JSTOR access blocked full text; not independently read. Not relied on for the phase count; accepted_age now cites S7 instead.

sources.citation: Gresky, J., Haelm, J., Clare, L. (2017). Modified human crania from Göbekli Tepe provide evidence for a new form of Neolithic skull cult. Science Advances 3(6): e1700564.
sources.note: Abstract read: three partly preserved skulls show artificial modifications unknown elsewhere in the period; burials are otherwise absent; interpreted as a new form of skull cult.

confidence_note: Age and pre-farming context are solidly sourced from open literature. features_at_claim covers the monumental/age claim; the 'purely ritual' reading, now split out, is covered by objections.
corrections: Commonly repeated detail that Benedict mistook pillar tops for grave markers is UNVERIFIED: S1's quotation of Benedict (1980: 179, 181) describes flint-strewn knolls with small cemeteries, not a grave-marker misreading.
The exact 1994 recognition date (before 1995 excavation) is UNVERIFIED in sources reviewed; this record codes 1995, when excavation and public reporting began, as year_claimed (S1).

The brief's 'domestic or roofed buildings' framing holds: Banning (2011, S4) proposed the enclosures could be houses; post-2014 fieldwork (S7) instead found separate domestic structures beside the decorated enclosures.
notes: This record separates two parts of the 1995 claim: (1) pre-agricultural hunter-gatherers built monumental enclosures c. 9600-8200 cal BC; (2) the complex was purely ritual, with no residents. Part (1) is vindicated; part (2) failed. Post-2014 excavation (S7) found domestic structures with hearths near the enclosures and a burial (DR1); S9's 2017 'burials absent' account predates this. S7 also found the fill is redeposited slope debris mixing PPNA/PPNB material, not deliberate backfill, explaining early dates' heterogeneity. 'May have helped drive the shift to agriculture' is untested and dropped from claim. No source suggests hoax or contamination; debate is about function, not age.

plates.caption: Overview of the main excavation area at Göbekli Tepe, showing stone enclosures with upright T-shaped pillars.

open_issues: multiple_labs and decisive_tests' 'second lab outside Kiel' premise rest on unverified 1998 dates (Kromer & Schmidt, Neo-Lithics 3/98); not independently located this round, left as in the draft.
S5 (Dietrich & Notroff 2015) and S8 (Kinzel & Clare 2020) remain paywalled beyond confirmed metadata; not relied on for key fields.

Whether an expectation of sedentism (e.g. Natufian villages) already existed pre-1995, versus being newly established here, is untested against a source like Bar-Yosef 1998; objections[1] left 'unresolved' rather than resolved either way.

D19 re-rating 2026-09-23: partial → vindicated — monumental building before farming is accepted; the 'temple, no residents' reading is split out as a candidate. year_resolved 2000 (first dated peer-reviewed report) is a judgment call.
